Fire Twice
Rajgarh. 2:15 AM. A black car without headlights rolls into the bus stand. Two men get out with a jerry can.
Rocky Bhatia sees them first. He's been sleeping on the bench for four nights with a stump under his pillow.
By the time the first match is struck, eleven tennis-ball cricketers are running at the car. The men drop the can and drive into a ditch.
The awning burns. Only the awning. Papa puts it out with a bucket of chai water and a word Maa pretends not to hear.
They get three steps. Then torches come on from both sides of the road. "Police. Drop it."
One of them starts talking before they've even been handcuffed. A name. Mehra. A phone number. A payment of two lakh rupees.
Video call. Papa's face, black with smoke, grinning like a boy.
They came. They left. The stall is fine. Your Maa is angrier than the fire was.
Listen to me. Play the final. If you lose because you're scared, they win. If you lose playing, that's just cricket.
And if anybody tells you to get out on purpose, you tell them your father sells chai, not wickets.
There's a knock. Kabir Sir. And behind him, a man in a plain grey shirt who flew fourteen hours with an empty file folder.
{first}. You look older. Good. We need him to send the instruction, on the day, to a device we control. And we need it to reach us before the ball is bowled.
Nobody in the team knows except the three of us. And Karan.
"Wire me. Like last time."
You've done this before.
"Use the cloned phone. He texts it in real time."
Ishita's gift.
"I'll handle it myself on the field."
No wires. No plans.
Good. Then all you have to do is the hardest part. Play cricket like nothing is happening.
Then I'll be in the stands, and I'll be praying. I don't usually pray.
Team sheet for the final, slipped under your door. You're at six. Karan has written one line on the back in pencil.
"If he texts me, I'll drop it. I have to. My son, champ. I'm sorry."
The stall survived. Now the final has to.
